one_paragraph_summary: Art's Associate-Justice decade (October 1995-2005), opening with Ramos's appointment and the single-most-quoted vignette: when Ramos later asked how he had finally passed the JBC, Art answered 'without irony: I did not do it. The Lord did.' The bench 'changed him -- and revealed him.' He wrote relentlessly; opinions poured from his chambers; 'decisions were not merely rendered; they were reasoned'; colleagues noticed 'clarity without arrogance, firmness without cruelty.' Justice Antonio Carpio later called him 'the most prolific writer of the Court'; more than a thousand decisions bore his name; he chaired divisions, led reform committees, and wrote books -- 'one each year -- as if compelled to account for his stewardship.' His judicial philosophy crystallized into a 'simple, audacious premise': 'The judiciary must protect liberty and nurture prosperity.' Law, he argued, was 'not merely restraint -- it was enablement': predictable justice encouraged economic growth, fair courts strengthened democracy, 'liberty without order was chaos; order without liberty was tyranny.' Closing two-word cliffhanger: 'Then history intruded.'
